NEGROES Threaten To Make Trouble At Hartford. CITIZENS PATROLLING TOWN. OUTBREAK GROWS OUT OF KILLING OF A NEGRO. WAS SHOT BY CITY MARSHAL. Started By Fight Between White Men, In Which One Man's Skull Was Broken. RACE WAR SEEMS PROBABLE.
Owensboro, Ky., May 16.—[Special.]—One hundred and fifty sullen negroes are grouped about the alleyways of the town of Hartford to-night. Andrew Render, one of their number, was shot down to-night by Marshal R. L. Paris. Paris is being guarded at the Sheriff's office by fifty deputies who have been sworn in to-night. Probably fifty more of the most prominent citizens of the town have given their services to Sheriff Cal. Keown and are patrolling the streets. Both sides are armed with rifles, shotguns and pistols. An outbreak on the part of the negroes can be expected at any moment. The white citizens swear that if a movement is made to take Paris every negro in Ohio county will be exterminated. The killing was brought about in a round-about way. A street fair has been in progress at Hartford all the week.

To-day several hundred people were in the town. Pendleton Hudson and James Wysong, two white men, engaged in a fight at 6:30 o'clock to-night. Hudson hit Wysong over the head with a chair and fractured his skull. Wysong was taken to a physician's office and given aid. Deputy Sheriff Cal. Keown was sent to arrest Hudson. When the man saw him coming he prepared to resist arrest. The deputy pulled his pistol and Hudson ran down the main street of the town. Keown fired two shots at him, neither of which took effect.

Several hundred people had congregated on the streets. One block away in an alley nearly fifty negroes were drinking. When they heard the shots they started toward the main street. Marshal Paris was in front of the negroes, and he thought they would cause trouble if they went where the fight had occurred. The Marshal told the negroes he would arrest them if they advanced. Render cursed him and said no one could arrest him. He made a motion to put his hand to his back pocket and Paris pulled his revolver and fired at close range. The negro fell dead in his tracks. Paris went at once to the Sheriff and gave himself up.

The news of the killing spread to the coal mines on the edge of town, and in a short while the streets of Hartford were swarming with negroes.

Render belonged to a secret lodge and the members said he had been shot down for nothing and they intended to mob Paris before morning. Every saloon in the town was closed. The prominent citizens were prompt to act or Paris would have been taken from the officers half an hour after the killing. Many of the Republicans have gone to the negroes and told them to go home, but it has had little effect on them. Render was a desperate character. Only a week ago he and his gang had Marshal Paris hemmed up and threatened to kill him. It was known that he was armed this afternoon. The negroes have been making threats against the white citizens for several weeks and the outbreak to-night was not unexpected.

No Fear of Race War.
LOUISVILLE, Ky., May 17.—No further disorder is reported from Hartford, Ky., where fears of a race war were entertained Saturday night on account of the killing of a negro by the town marshal. The extra police force remains on duty, but the danger of an attempt on the part of the negroes to lynch the officer is apparently over.

NEGRO KILLED. Marshal Paris Shot Andy Render While the Latter Was Ad- vancing Upon Him.
A killing occurred in Hartford Saturday night which marred the otherwise pleasant record of the street fair. It was between 7 and 8 o'clock when the trouble came up. The crowds had dispersed and only a few strangers were left in Hartford, including a crowd of negroes from the mines at McHenry. Pendleton Hudson and Jim Wysong, two white men, became involved in a drunken brawl at Nall's saloon. Hudson struck Wysong over the head with a chair and escaped before he could be arrested. Marshal Enon Paris came up at this juncture and arrested Wysong. A crowd of darkies were standing near Griffin's corner and one of them asked Paris in a rough manner why he did not arrest the fellow who had skipped.

Just then Andy Render and several other darkies came along from the saloon. They were very boisterous and started down the alley past Griffin's corner. Two darkies had hold of Render, one on each side. He appeared to want to break loose and come back to where Marshal Paris was standing on the corner. More darkies came along and as they went down the alley they created considerable disturbance. One of them remarked that no Marshal would ever arrest him. At this time the crowd had gotten down the alley near Chinn's saloon. Marshal Paris went about half way down the alley and called to the darkies to make less noise. He pleaded with them that there had been no trouble so far during the two days of the fair and begged them to not let the event end up in a row. He told them he would have to arrest some of them if they did not get quiet.

Andy Render then walked out from the crowd of negroes towards Marshal Paris and said in a tantalizing way that he'd be d—d if the Marshal could arrest him. He kept advancing towards Marshal Paris in a threatening manner, with one hand behind him. Paris thought his life was in danger and just before Render got to him he thrust his pistol out and shot the darkey in the breast. The bullet pierced Render's heart and he died instantly.

Marshal Paris went straight and gave himself up to Sheriff C. P. Keown. There was considerable excitement down the alley for a little while. Several darkies went to Render to hold him up, but he was already dead. There was no weapon found upon him, but it is said he displayed a pistol only a short while before the shooting. He had the reputation of being a desperate darkey and had several times threatened Marshal Paris' life. He with other darkies got into trouble with Marshal Paris several weeks ago, and the Marshal's life was in great danger then. He had to call upon the Sheriff to help him quell the mob. One of the negroes was heard to remark shortly before the shooting that there was going to be "trouble in this old town to-night."

The above account of the shooting is the sum and substance of the affair as given to a HERALD reporter by Marshal Paris. The excitement did not last long and was in no wise of such a sensational character as depicted in several city papers by some irresponsible reporter here. Render lay where he fell for about an hour and there was great wailing among the darkies. About nine o'clock his remains were taken to McHenry in an express wagon.

Marshal Paris has been in the hands of guards since the shooting and his case will probably be taken up by the grand jury, now in session here, some time this week.

Speech In Lindle Case To Be Made To-day. MUCH INTEREST MANIFESTED IN THE WARM LEGAL BATTLE AT MADISONVILLE. GRAYOT TO CLOSE ARGUMENT.
Madisonville, Ky., May 21.—[Special.]

Four speeches were made in the Lindle case to-day, two for the Commonwealth and two for the defense. Judge Julian limited the time of the speakers to two hours each. County Attorney Ruby Laffoon made the opening this morning, which was the second argument in the case, J Fletcher Dempsey having spoken yesterday afternoon. He was followed by Judge Breathitt, of Hopkinsville, for the defense. The speeches this afternoon were made by the Hon. W. H. Yost, of Greenville, for the prosecution, and Congressman Ollie M. James, of Marion, for the defense. Commonwealth's Attorney Grayot will conclude the arguments to-morrow morning. This is one of the warmest legal fights that has been made in years and the attorneys put forth their best efforts. The court room was crowded with spectators throughout the day.

FARMER FOUND DEAD.

Coroner Believes Death Was Due To Ruptured Blood Vessel.

Ruptured Blood Vessel.

Henderson, Ky., May 21.—[Special.]—M. L. Schaeffer, a farmer, was found dead on the island below this city this morning, and the cause of his death is a mystery. He was driving a team of four mules to a roller at 6 o'clock yesterday evening and was in good health. His failure to go home last night caused a search this morning, and his body was found lying in the field with blood all about it. The mules were standing near him still attached to the roller. There were no marks of violence about his body and the Coroner thinks ruptured blood vessel caused this death. Schaeffer was fifty years old. He had no relatives here.

CONTEST CASE CONTINUED.

An Effort To Oust Johnson County's Only Democratic Official.

Painttsville, Ky., May 21.—[Special.]—In the Circuit Court to-day the case of Jethro Preston against J. M. Price, the present County Clerk of this county, was passed until July 7, when Judge Auxler will hear the case at Pikeville. This case, which involves the County Court Clerkship, went against Preston at the last term of Circuit Court. He took an appeal and the case was reversed and remanded on account of a technicality in the pleadings. Mr. Price is the first Democratic clerk of this county since its formation and the only Democratic official in twenty years. His majority over Preston was about twenty.

MRS. NASH'S DAMAGE SUIT

Against Officials of Shelbyville Is Now On Trial.

Shelbyville, Ky., May 21.—[Special.]—The most notable suit on the docket of the present term of Circuit Court is now on trial. It is the case of Mrs. Kate Frazier Nash, of Louisville, against the city of Shelbyville and individual Councilmen and the directors of the Shelbyville Public Library for $10,000 damages for alleged desecration of the graves of plaintiff's relatives.

When required to elect this afternoon the attorneys of the plaintiff released all the defendants except Mayor L. C. Willis, John I. Logan and F. Moesser, The case is being warmly contested.

LOOKING FOR HUSBAND.

Mrs. N. M. Dowell Calls On Owensboro Police For Assistance.

Owensboro, Ky., May 21.—Mrs. N. M. Dowell, of Louisville, is in the city looking for her husband, who has been living here for several months while his wife lived in Louisville. He wrote her last week that he was going to leave and Saturday night he gave up his job and has not been seen since. He was employed in a clothing store and had built up an excellent reputation as a salesman. Mrs. Dowell says that he gave no reason for leaving her. She has reported the matter to the police, who will make every effort to locate Dowell.

Owingsville, Ky., May 21.—[Special.]
—Hugh Pergram, while hunting in the eastern part of this county, found a meteorite. The body had crashed through two limbs of a tree and buried itself in the ground. Hoped That President Loubet Will Not Ask to See the

Pope.

Rome, June 9.—The negotiations between the Vatican and France regarding the attitude to be assumed by President Loubet towards the Pope during the President's coming visit to Rome are at a standstill. The Vatican hopes a change will occur by France modifying the situation. If no change takes place the idea prevails that M. Loubet will not ask to see the Pope, thus avoiding a refusal, which would necessarily bring about a rupture between France and the Vatican. The authorities believe that by M. LYNCHED HIS SLAYER
W. COPE WINSLOW. JR., AVENGED AT FORT VALLEY.
KILLED BY BANJO PEAVY.
NEGRO WAS TAKEN FROM THE SHERIFF AND HANGED.
Negro Owed Winslow, Who Asked Him to Work Out the Debt—He Shot Winslow Through the Head. Winslow Fired at Peavy as the Negro Fled—Posse Was Organized and Captured the Negro, Who Was Later Taken Away from His Guards—Hanged in the Town.

Macon, Ga., June 8.—W. Cope Winslow, Jr., whose father was one of the leading members of the Georgia bar, was instantly killed by a negro named Banjo Peavy on the former's farm near Fort Valley at 2 o'clock this afternoon.

The negro owed Mr. Winslow a small amount of money and was asked to work out the debt. He refused impudently and shot Mr. Winslow through the forehead.

Before Mr. Winslow died he fired twice at his fleeing assassin without effect.

When the news was brought to town a posse was organized and the country searched. The negro was soon captured and turned over to the sheriff.

Body Was Riddled.

At 8:30 o'clock to-night the officer and guard were overpowered and the negro taken to a grove within the corporate limits, where he was hanged and his body riddled with bullets.

The dead young man was the main support of his widowed mother and three sisters.

Officers Did Not Resist.

There was no determined resistance on the part of the officers, who were at a great disadvantage. While Fort Valley is the largest city of the county, Perry is the county seat, and Peavy was being held, awaiting transportation. The mob was business-like, coupling their demand with a threat.

The place where the negro was hanged is known as Branham's Grove. After he was swung up, about 300 bullets were fired into the pendant body.

The major portion of the town was surprised by the fusillade, and consternation prevailed. The older and wiser citizens are said to deplore the event.

A Brutal Crime Is Avenged Last Night.
A LYNCHING AT FORT VALLEY.
W. Cope Winslow is Brutally Murdered By a Negro-Enraged Citizens Captured Black Fiend and Promptly Strung Him Up.
In the presence of scores of Fort Valley's citizens, Sandy Williams was roped into eternity at 8:30 o'clock last night for the brutal killfng of Mr. W. Cope Winslow, a prominent young man of the town, which bloody crime was committed there just after noon yesterday.

Hundreds saw the black brute die last night for his heinous crime.

For eight hours determined men hunted him over field and through swamp, and when at last the cowering wretch was run to cover his doom was sealed in a moment.

For fifteen miles the determined band of men chased the murderer. Williams was armed with a rifle and two pistols, one of which he used in killing Mr. Winslow, but this fact did not deter those who wanted his blood for the horrible murder committed.

When at last his capture was effected Williams was carried back to Fort Valley, marched to a livery stable and lynched.

Older citizens counseled the crowd, but to no effect. They knew the laws delay and how so often justice is defeated. They knew that the prisoner had murdered in cold blood one of their best citizens. What the need of months of delay, and the possibility of escape.

And thus the black brute was put to instant death at the rope.

No tragedy of recent years had so stirred a community. Without provocation the negro had approached Mr. Winslow, as he sat in his buggy in front of his gate, and renewed a previous difficulty. The negro was armed with a pistol and weeding hoe.

The men had had trouble early in the day when Williams, armed with a pistol, defied Mr. Winslow, who was then unarmed.

In the afternoon Williams came back to Mr. Winslow's house, and renewed the trouble.

Winslow, it is said, fired twice at Williams, but the plunging of his horse caused him to miss the mark. At this juncture the negro fired once, the bullet entering Mr. Winslow's forehead, killing him instantly, the dead body falling out of the buggy.

Williams fled, but was captured after a long chase. The rest of the story is told above.

Mr. Winslow was 23 years of age, single, and the main support of a widowed mother. He was a nephew of Mr. E. J. McGehee of Americus and well known here. THE CASE OF WILLIS.
EVEN TEXAS JUSTICE, which is sometimes singularly blind so far as the rights of negroes are concerned, should uphold the action of Bob Willis of Henderson, who fired into a mob that came to whip him and killed one member of it, besides seriously wounding another. An account of the affair says that Willis, who is a negro, is in the hands of the sheriff. Just why he should be under arrest we are at a loss to understand.

Willis did exactly what any other man would have done under the same circumstances. He defended his home and himself from an attack by a gang of lawless desperadoes. It was necessary, in this defense, for him to fire upon his assailants. The fact that he killed one of them by no means makes him a criminal in any sense of the word. The law gives every man the right to protect his home, to go to any lengths in order to preserve it. The law also gives a man the right to protect his life.

The dispatch from Henderson gives the impression that Willis had done something the mob didn't like. Just what his offense was is not made clear, but the mob determined to whip him. The attempt was made, with the result already stated. Then Willis was arrested by the sheriff because he defended himself and his home from the mob. It is to be hoped that he will be freed at once. But the chances are that he will be obliged to leave the country for he is a marked man now. At the earliest possible moment some friend of the outlaw who was killed will kill Willis. So his freedom, as far as Henderson, Tex., is concerned, will be of little value to him. The case of Willis is a most unfortunate one.

TORTURE OF NEGROES.
Collector Flanagan Reports Terrible Crueltles Perpetrated in Rusk County. Tex.
AUSTIN, Tex., Oct. 14.—Webster Fianagan, United States Collector of Internal Revenue for this district, returned to-day from Rusk county, in this State, where he went several days ago to investigate the murders and cruelties that are being perpetrated upon the negroes of that county by bands of white men.

"No one can portray the cruelties to which the negroes of Rusk county have been subjected during the past several weeks," Mr. Flanagan said to-day. "I have laid the matter before Gov. Lanham, with a view of bringing about the punishment of those who are guilty. If necessary, an appeal will be made to the Federal authorities.

"A few nights before my visit to the county two of the most peaceable and inoffensive negroes were taken from their homes by a band of white men. They were stripped and tied to trees and then whipped with the most terrible instrument of torture ever devised by savage man. This instrument was a broad strip of rawhide fastened on to an oak handle. Nails were driven through the rawhide, protruding nearly a half inch. The negroes were whipped into insensibility with these lashes, each stroke driving the nails into the cringing body. One of these negroes died last Saturday night from his injuries and the other one is in a critical condition. The men who committed this crime are well known. Four of them have been arrested.

"The order has gone forth that all negroes must leave the county. The only excuse given for the murder and outrages that have been committed is that it is a white man's county. Many negroes have obeyed the warning and moved away."

Outrages in Rusk County, Tex., Declared to Be Unparalleled.

Capture of a Negro Boy Charged With a Serious Crime.

Columbus, Ga., May 22.—With a rope tied around his neck to prevent him from escaping, Calvin Baker, a 15-year-old negro boy, who is charged with having made an attempt to criminally assault the 5-year-old daughter of Mr. Richard Thedford, at Knight's Station, was brought to Phenix City this morning.

He was captured near Crawford, Ala., ten miles east of the city, at 6 o'clock this morning. The boy's capture was effected by strategy. After the attempted outrage Wednesday night, he ran away, and it was suspected that he had gone to Crawford. Mr. Thedford followed and found that the boy had applied for work on the farm of Mr. Foster there.

The two men had a conference, and this morning Mr. Foster told the boy to do some work in a crib. When he stepped inside, Mr. Foster locked the door, making him a prisoner.

Baker was carried to the county seat of Lee county, Opelika, this afternoon.

Clarendon, July 1.—The troubles out in the Fowler-Coburn neighborhood, beginning with the killing of Fowler and culminating with the lynching of Harris, the assailant of Coburn, have now developed a financial side. The negroes of that neighborhood have received anonymous letters setting forth that "the quickest way out of the country was the best," and a general exodus of negroes seemed imminent.

Most of the plantations in the disturbed district are the property of men residing in this city. Hearing that they were likely to be deprived of their black labor through the intimidation of unknown parties a number of them went out to the fearridden community yesterday afternoon with the hope of quieting the fears of the negroes and persuading them to remain on the places. On promise of protection from their landlords and the best citizens of that section, the darkies have consented to stay. The owners of the farms worked by the frightened blacks were much concerned because of the considerable loss their leaving would have occasioned.

It is generally believed that the intimidatory letters were the work of some irresponsible white renters who hoped, by producing a scarcity of labor, to cheapen rents. The better class of white farmers are anxious to have order restored and are sorry that a few reckless ones should earn for the community a reputation for lawlessness.

eugene-smith-liberty-1903-07-12.A1:
NEGRO ATTACKS A CHILD.
Citizens of Liberty, This State. Barely Prevent a Lynching.
[BY TELEGRAPH TO THE TRIBUNE.]

Liberty, N. Y., July 13.—Eugene Smith, a negro porter in Robert Jacobs's boarding house, about 9:30 p. m. Sunday broke into the room occupied by Mrs. E. H. Clarke and her two little girls, aged seven and eight years. It is charged that the negro seized the younger child by the throat and was attacked by Mrs. Clarke, who called to her children to alarm Harry L. May, the boarder in the next room. They succeeded in getting out, and then Mrs. Clarke broke away and ran to the room.

The negro followed and attempted to enter. His fingers were caught in the door and his screams aroused the household. At last he got away.

Several persons, frightened, had taken refuge in Jacobs's apartments.

The negro, scantily dressed, hurried to the street. A crowd of about one thousand persons stood around the house. Smith was struck with clubs and roughly handled. There were cries of "Lynch him!" Citizens then took Smith from the mob and hurried him to jail. The officer in charge addressed the excited people, urging them to go quietly to their homes and let the law take its course. The leaders at last persuaded the crowd to disperse.

It was found that the electric wires in the house had been cut before Mrs. Clarke's room was entered.

MIDDLETOWN, N. Y., July 14.—Two little girls, aged six and eight years, of Liberty, Sullivan county, were attacked Sunday night by Eugene Smith, a negro, formerly of New York. Smith narrowly escaped lynching at the hands of an infuriated mob which gathered when the news of his attempted crime became known.

The negro had a hearing before Judge Grant, and an adjournment was taken until today. He persistently refused to say anything concerning himself.

Mr. Robert Cheatham Seriously Wounded-Would-be Assassins Supposed to be Negroes of Phoenix Section.
[The State.]

Mr. Cheatham received a charge of buckshot in the upper part of his body, his hands, arms and chest receiving the load. Although at close range his physician thinks that the wounds are not necessarily fatal. He will recover unless some complications set in.

Mr. Quattlebaum had his left arm broken and also received some flesh wounds in the upper part of the body.

Mr. Penn's wound was made by a charge of bird skot which centered in the calf of the left leg.

ELEVEN TAKEN TO HELENA FOR EXAMINATION ON THAT CHARGE.
Charged That They Entered Saw Mill Operated by Negroes and Closed It Down.
Wynne, Ark., Aug. 21.—Deputy United States Marshal U. G. Copeland passed through Wynne this morning with eleven prisoners, charged with whitecapping, at White Hall, Poinsett county, Ark. On the morning of August 17. J. R. Parker, John T. Parker, Rube Parker, Will Stafford, Clyde Stafford, J. H. Harrison (school teacher), S. W. McKinney, W. R. Clampit, Will England, Lee Bridges and Charles Blake, all white, and most of them well to do planters of Poinsett county, entered the sawmill belonging to Davis and Hodges, which is operated exclusively by negro labor, and ordered the negroes from the mill, threatening them with violence if they did not leave at once. The negroes promptly complied with the orders of the whitecappers. This occurred about 10 o'clock in the morning. All of the above named men went to the mill in a body, unmasked, and gave the orders, thus shutting the mill down. Messrs. Davis and Hodges have been forced to suspend business temporarily and are leaving nothing unturned towards prosecuting the guilty parties. Attorney Clyde Going of Harrisburg, Ark., accompanied the prisoners to Helena, and will represent them before United States Commissioner E. R. Crum. It is believed they will waive examination and give bond for their appearance at the October term of court. Messrs. Davis and Hodges think it is the work of some personal enemies, or grudge that some of the citizens have against them, as no other negroes were bothered, and the community is thickly populated with negroes. Messrs. Davis and Hodges are both highly respected gentlemen. Owing to the friendship and relatives on both sides, it is feared that serious trouble will be the final result.

Special Dispatch to the Evening Star.

RICHMOND, Va., June 5.—Cumberland, Va., June 5.—Whitecaps have been at work in this neighborhood as the result of the corts declining to take from the guardianship of Fleming and Amanda Brown, co-ored, a dwarf girl named Rosa Taylor.

The girl is sixteen years old, stunted and weakly, yet she was so badly beaten by her guardian several weeks ago that her garments were cemented to her skin with her own blood, and for nine days the stripes and bruises were visible on her body.

Neighbors, who had heard the terrible tale from the dwarf's lips, took the case to court, but the guardians managed to get the child retained in their care, and the court's instructions to them were to whip her when she needed it, but not cruelly.

This made the neighbors determined to take the matter in their hands, and a committee of safety was organized. This committee went to the house of the Browns near Ashby at 1 o'clock one morning recently, and it is reported that they made Fleming Brown pay well for his cruelty. The "committee of safety," it is said, have several other matters to look into.

LAKE VILLAGE, Ark., Nov. 3.—Two people are dead and three wounded as the result of trouble between the whites and blacks here to-day, which was not settled until a lynching had quieted the excited people.

—The Dead.—

FRANK ANDERSON, white, Lake Village, killed in fight.

HENRY JOHNSON, a negro, lynched at noon.

—Wounded.—

B. VINSON, white, a lawyer of Little Rock.

JOSEPH FRAME, white, of Lake Village.

ELLA M'DOWELL, colored.

A row occurred between some negroes and whites early in the day. It is claimed that during the altercation Ed Coleman, colored, drew a revolver and began shooting. A fusilade followed, and when it ceased it was found that Frank Anderson, one of those in the crowd, was dead, Vinson was shot in two places, Joseph Frame wounded in the foot, and Ella McDowell, colored, shot in the back. Coleman fled and a posse at once started in pursuit. Johnson, one of the negroes in the crowd, was arrested and placed in jail.

Excitement ran high among the people, and increased until noon, when the courthouse bell sounded and most of the white citizens assembled. A number of speeches was made and a committee on law enforcement was appointed. The question was raised as to what should be done with the negro Johnson. It was announced that Circuit Judge Wood would be in town soon to hold a special term of court, and that the case could be heard then, but a large number of those present rushed out of the courthouse, shouting "Hang him! hang him!" Sledge hammers and railroad irons were quickly found, and in thirty minutes four doors at the jail had been broken down. The mob quickly secured the negro, took him to the center of town and hanged him at noon.

LAKE VILLAGE TRAGEDY.
Frank Anderson Killed, and Baldy Vinson Seriously Wounded.
Dermott, Ark., Nov. 4.—Word was received here yesterday of the death of Frank Anderson, a prominent business man of Lake Village, and the shooting of Baldy Vinson, the well-known Little Rock attorney. Joe Frame was also wounded. Anderson was killed instantly and Vinson's wounds are supposed to be fatal. Two negroes of the name of Henry Johnson and Ed. Coleman are responsible for the death of Anderson and the wounding of the other two men. Johnson made no effort to escape, and was arrested soon after the shooting occurred. Coleman ran and has not been apprehended.

The shooting took place about 2 o'clock in the morning, and as near as can be ascertained, it occurred in Frame's wine room. Frame was shot in the foot and will recover. It is feared that Vinson's wounds will prove fatal.

Baldy Vinson, who is engaged in the practice of law in Little Rock, left for Lake Village only two days ago. He formerly lived there and is one of the most prominent young attorneys in southeastern Arkansas.

Frank Anderson is Killed "Baldy" Vinson is Shot in the Arm and Joe Frame Wounded.

LYNCHING AT LAKE VILLAGE
Follows a Battle in Saloon Between Whites and Blacks
IN WHICH FRANK ANDESON WAS KILLED
A Prominent Little Rock Lawyer was Wounded in the Affray-No Further Trouble Anticipated By Officers.
Little Rock, Ark., Nov. 4.—A dispatch from Lake Village states that at noon yesterday the steel jail was entered by an infuriated crowd of men who took Henry Johnson, colored, from his cell and hanged him in the center of the town.

The lynching was the result of a shooting affray which occurred in a saloon between negroes on one side and whites on the other.

Frank Anderson, white, was instantly killed and Baldy Vinson, a well known lawyer of Little Rock, received two wounds, but he will recover. Two other parties were injured but not seriously.

The trouble is said to have been brought on by the action of negro waiters in the saloon. Anderson is said to have resented some remarks made by one of the negroes. With Anderson were several friends, including Baldy Vinson and Joe Frame. The first shot was fired by Ed Coleman, a negro, and then followed a regular fusillade. When the battle ceased it was found that the results were that Anderson was dead with several bullets in his body; that Vinson was shot in two places, and that Joe Frame was shot in the foot. Of the negroes engaged in the affray it was found that Ella McDowell had been shot, the ball entering her back and lodging in the breast.

Ed Coleman, the negro who fired the first shot, fled, but it is hardly possible for him to escape.

Henry Johnson, the party who was lynched, was captured and placed in jail.

The shooting caused the greatest excitement, and at noon Tuesday the crowd assembled in the court house yard and demanded that the prisoner be handed over to them.

Conservative citizens pleaded with the crowd to let the law take its course, and a sum was subscribed to defray the expense of prosecuting the negroes, but this did not satisfy the people. Sledge hammers were secured and in a few minutes the jail doors were battered down. The mob then entered the jail, seized the frightened negro Johnson, took him to the lake front in the center of the town and swung him up. Not a shot was fired by the mob, which quickly dispersed after accomplishing its intention. The negro's body remained hanging for several hours and was finally cut down by the coroner.

Chicot county, of which Lake Village is the county seat, has a large negro population, the blacks outnumbering the whites about five to one, but there is no fear of further trouble as all the officers are white men and have heretofore been able to keep down any serious race trouble. Sheriff Frank Strong was in Little Rock when the shooting and lynching occurred, but on receipt of the news left at once for home.

Police Convinced That He's the Man Who Stole Ruby Steele.
The Girl Identifies Him and He Can't Account for His Time.
Feeling Runs High and the Prisoner Is Being Carefully Guarded.
Extra precaution will be taken by the police, ten-night to protect James Hayes, the negro who is charged with stealing 13-year-old Ruby Steele from her room at 1414 Sixth street SE early this morning and attempting to assault her. Feeling is high and the police will guard the station to-night with an extra detail.

Hayes crouches in a corner of cell No. 1 at the central station and his teeth chatter with fear when he hears any unusual sound. He starts suddenly when addressed and at times his lips tremble until he is scarcely able to speak. He maintains his innocence, but is unable to explain how his handkerchief came to be in the girl's room and can only give a lame explanation for not staying in his own room last night. He says he was in St. Paul all night, but a man was found by the police who saw the negro board a St. Paul car shortly after the assault. The police say that they have such evidence against the negro that he cannot escape conviction.

How Hayes Was Arrested.

Hayes was arrested this morning by Detective J. G. Doyle and C. D. Brown. They found a handkerchief in the girl's room which bore the laundry marks "F. A. B." This handkerchief was identified by Frank A. Benjamin, Hayes' employer, as one that had been given the colored man. The detectives then went to Hayes' room and found that the bed had been unoccupied. They sent a general alarm to all the stations and to all officers, as well as to St. Paul. Then they went to the Benjamin barn, where Hayes works, and awaited developments. Shortly before 6 o'clock they heard the sound of a key in the barn lock and an instant later the negro stepped in.

The suspect was at once confronted by the two officers, who began to question him. He told them that he had been in St. Paul, where he slept in the room of a friend. This friend, he said, had left the city early this morning and had gone out on the breakbeams of a freight train. He said that the absent friend was the one who had stolen the girl from her room, but when the handerchief was shown him, he was at a loss to explain how it came to be in the room. The detectives decided to question no further and Hayes was arrested and charged with the crime.

A Desperate Attempt.

The crime attempted was one of the most atrocious in the history of the city. About 1 o'clock this morning a negro entered the room of Ruby Steele and literally stole her. It was only after the mother was knocked down that Hayes succeeded in getting away with the girl, and but for the prompt arrival of several men awakened by the mother's screams, the case would have been even more serious.

The girl's room was in the rear of the second story of her home nad directly beneath the window is the roof of a summer kitchen. The negro climbed to this roof and made his way to her window. He carefully removed the screen and went to the girl's side, placing a handkerchief saturated with chloroform over her face. The girl awoke and screamed for help. The negro placed his hand over her mouth and started to drag her thru the window. Her cries attracted her mother, who seized the girl by the foot as she was being dragged thru the window. She maintained her hold until the negro dealt her a stunning blow in the face and knocked her down.

He then dragged the terrorized girl to the edge of the roof and threw her to the ground, a distance of several feet. He jumped after her and picking her up in his arms, ran thru a small corn patch to the barn, where he is employed. He then threw the girl on the ground and sat on her body, keeping his hand over her mouth to prevent her from making any out cry. He listened for pursuers but did not hear any one approaching. The girl then began to fight for her liberty and the negro choked her almost to insensibility.

Rescued by Neighbors.

Just as the girl was about to give up her struggles, a neighbor who had been aroused by the girl's cries, approached and her assailant disappeared in the darkness. A good description was secured of him and the Steele girl was able to identify Hayes.

The girl is hysterical to-day. She did not realize the man's brutal purpose until she had been rescued. Her injuries consist of a few cuts from broken glass, several painful bruises and a few scratches. Her throat shows discolorations where the brute choked her.

Hayes' Record Bad.

Hayes seems to have a mania for assaulting women, as this is the second attempt he has been accused of in Minneapolis, altho he says he has been in the city only four weeks. The other attempt was made upon Miss Arunga Burres, a domestic employed in the household of F. A. Benjamin, 700 Fifteenth avenue SE. Hayes was employed by Benjamin and occupied a room in his employer's residence. About a week ago Miss Burres, who has a room on the upper floor of the residence, ran screaming down the stairs to Mrs. Benjamin's room. She said that Hayes had entered her room and had thrown a quilt over her head and tried to gag her. She had fought him off. A few scratches about her face were evidence of the truth of her story.

Hayes said he had not been in the girl's room, but that he had heard her scream and presumed she had night mare. Mr. Benjamin believed the negro's story, but at the instigation of his wife and daughters he secured the negro a room on Fourteenth avenue near Sixth street, less than a block from where the assault was attempted last night.

Hayes is an inferior looking negro, being of small stature, with a receding forehead and thick lips. He is blacker than most negroes seen in the north and seems to be very illiterate. He says that he is 27 years old and was born in Columbia, Mo., but has lived at 1908 Cherry street, Kansas City, Mo., for several years. He also says he was in Sloux City, Iowa, for several days before coming to Minneapolis.

Mrs. Steele is very nervous to-day as a result of the excitement, while her face is badly swollen from the blow she received. She was alone with the children, Ruby and another daughter, the father, J. P. Steele, being at Warroad, Minn.

HAYES HELD TO G. J.
Negro Charged With Assault Has Preliminary Hearing To-day.
The Evidence Is Conflicting, and He May Get Off Alto-gether.
Disappointment was felt this morning over the weakness of the case of the state against James Hayes, the colored man charged with second degree assault upon 13-year-old Ruby Steele. This weakness was due in a large measure to the disagreement in essential details of the stories told by the girl and her mother, as well as the disagreement of the stories told in direct and cross-examinations. While there is a chance for the state to convict Hayes yet there also remains a chance that he will go free.

The girl was the first witness called by the state and told the story just about as given in The Journal for Monday. She was unable to tell what part of her body the colored man had hold of when he dragged her from her room and thru the cornfield. Upon cross-examination, F. L. McGee, Hayes' attorney, drew out several important admissions. Among these were the statements that she weighs 132 pounds and is only 13 years old; that she never smelled chloroform and yet knew that Hayes' handkerchief was saturated with the drug; that her throat was covered with cuts and scratches but that all traces of them had disappeared since Monday, and that altho she was dragged nearly a block thru tall grass wet with dew, her clothing was perfectly dry and was not changed until Tuesday or Wednesday.

The state then put Mrs. Steele, mother of the girl, on the stand and she told of having heard her daughter call for help. She had run to the room only to receive several hard blows from her daughter's assailant. She then saw Ruby and the colored man fall off the roof and saw him drag the girl into the corn, where she could hear them scuffling. Later her daughter came back, her clothing all covered with blood and dirt, but on cross-examination she said that the soiled clothing was not discarded for fresh men until two days later.

Attorney McGee then stipulated with the county attorney that the charge against Hayes was that of assault in the second degree, brought under the section which provides that an assault committed while attempting another crime is assault in the second degree. He then submitted the case without offering any testimony on the part of the defense and Judge Dickinson held Hayes to the grand jury in $5,000 bail.

The charge of second degree assault materially lightens the matter and makes the maximum penalty for Hayes, provided he is convicted, only five years, while if the charge of attempted rape had been maintained, he might have been given fifteen years in prison.

Jim Gilmore was captured at Pursley & Parrott's saw mill, near King's Mountain last Tuesday evening by Sheriff Logan and Messrs. Calvin Pursley and C. F. Gordon.

Gilmore is the negro who was arrested at Lowryville last year on the charge of having broken into a house occupied by some unprotected ladies. The authorities here, fearing an attempt at lynching, telegraphed Governor Ayeck for authority to call out the troops. This was granted, and the Gate City Guards are at this hour—midnight—in their armory prepared for any emergency.

CONDITION OF MISS WALKER.
Mr. Blair Buried---Further Details Concerning the Murder Near Reidsville.
(Special to News and Observer.)

Reidsville, N. C., March 21.—Sheriff Frank Pinnix and J. E. Lambeth have returned from Greensboro, where they carried Broadnax, the murderer of Sidney Blair. They did not accompany him to Raleigh.

The crime was the general topic of conversation throughout the county. Many are of opinion that if the negro had not been removed from the county jail he would have been lynched. Others think there was more talk than anything else. The remains of Mr. Blair were buried today. A large concourse of friends and relatives attended the funeral.

The impression is that Mr. Blair kept large sums of money hidden on the premises. Broadnax was acquainted with the premises and the old man's habits and knew where some money had been hidden. The negro chose the time for attack well. No trains were passing at that hour and the nearest neighbors living at some distance could be counted upon as doing the evening's work at home. There was darkness enough to hide his movements and make escape probable.

Miss Walker is resting easy today. She was only wounded in two places.

JURORS TO TRY BROADNX.
Extraordinary Bravery Displayed by Miss Walker---The Negro's Coolness.
(Warner) The Nes and Observer.)

(Special to Nes and Observer.)

Reidsville, N. C. March 22 - The Coy

Reidsville, N. C., March 23.—The County Commissioners were in session to-day and drew off a list of jurors for the special term of Rockingham Superior court, which Governor Aycock has ordered for the trial of John Broadnax, the colored youth who killed Mr. Sidney Blair and wounded Miss Sallie Walker on last Thursday night. It is not known which judge will preside, but the trial will probably only take up a few hours' time.

The citizens here continue to discuss the tragedy. The young woman's bravery comes in for the largest share of the conversation. No one will ever know the extent of her bravery until they visit the scene and become acquainted with the facts. She is able to be up and she thinks she will be entirely well in a few days' time. A few minutes after she was shot she left for a neighbor's house, a distance of one mile, for help. How she managed to get there is a mystery. She was weak from the loss of blood, and she thinks she must have fallen at least a dozen times.

The coolness of the negro has also impressed all who have seen him. While Deputy Sheriff Faucette and Mr. Glass were with the negro ready to start for the Wentworth jail, Broadnax asked the gentlemen to tie his bicycle on the rear of the buggy; he might have need for it later on, and ere they were ten feet from the Blair home the prisoner was whistling a familiar negro tune. He seemed perfectly contented in the Wentworth jail, but was delighted when informed that he would be carried to Greensboro and Raleigh; pleased with the idea that he was to see something of the world.

NEGRO MURDERS AN OLD MAN. Then Shoots a Woman Who Defends Herself and is Not Killed.
The darkest crime in the annals of Rockingham county was committed Thursday night in the Carmel section, five miles from Reidsville, when John Broadnax, a negro boy, sixteen years old, killed Sidney Blair, and estimable citizen of sixty, and shot Miss Sallie Walker three times. Miss Walker is a school teacher and kept house for Blair who is her uncle.

The murderer was captured and carried to jail in a few hours after the commission of the crime. Miss Walker told the story of the crime to a correspondent of the Charlotte Observer as follows:

"While we were eating supper John Broadnax, a negro boy about 16 years old, entered the dining room. He engaged in a conversation with Uncle Sidney, and then pulled out a revolver and commenced firing at me. Two shots took effect, one of the bullets entering at the skin of my neck, and the other grazing my side. I arose and as I did so he aimed at my uncle. We were then all standing in a few feet of each other around the table. He fired two shots at my uncle, one ball entering the collar-bone, and the other pierced his bowels. We followed the negro to the door he entered, closing the door behind him and latched it as he went out. Mr. Blair wanted to open the door and follow Broadnax, but I stopped him, fearing that he would be shot again. Uncle asked, 'Where did the ball hit you?' Before I could answer, or ask him where he was hit, he fell without speaking again or uttering another sound. As we followed the negro to the door he continued firing at us. When he left I fastened the door, but hearing me scream or or make a noise he entered and unfastened the door and began firing at me again. I succeeded in pushing him out and told him not to dare enter again. Previous to that time I had never been uneasy when the negro came around. Even when he entered the kitchen that night I didn't fear him any more than I would have feared a cat, and not as much as I would have feared a strange dog. The negro had worked for my uncle and was acquainted with his habits and the premises. A few weeks ago some one robbed my uncle of between $50 and $80, and it is believed that Broadnax was the perpetrator of that crime. After blowing the light out and getting quiet I heard a noise at the front door. The negro was there try- it flashed upon me that the negro had committed the murder in order to succeed in robbing the premises. I extinguished the light in order to escape without injury and to obtain help for my uncle. I remained quiet until the negro entered the house. After remaining quiet a short while I heard him in the hall or front room, and thought then it was my opportunity to escape and secure aid for my uncle. I slipped off my shoes and started toward the eastern door, not knowing but what some one was standing there ready to kill me, but I took the chances. I used all the strength in my power to reach the neighbor, the nearest one living a mile, and after many many hard falls, I finally succeeded. Mr. Estes was not at home, but his nephew went after him and soon carried him to our home. They
hephew went after him and soon carried him to our home. They found the negro in the house pillaging. Other neighbors were sent for. Broadnax attempted to escape, but a guard fired at him and he remained in the house. The negro succeeded in finding $5 87, and was ransacking trunks when captured. My surmise is that he thought there was a lot of money there but since the last robbery my uncle had removed his money.

Governor Aycock has ordered a special term of court on April 13 to try the negro.

BROADNAX TAKEN TO REIDSVILLE.
To be Tried for the Murder of Sidney Blair
Last Month.
John Broadnax, the 16-year-old mulatto who has been in Wake county jail for some time for safe keeping, was taken to Reidsville yesterday.

Court begins there on Monday and the special term will be presided over by Judge B. F. Long, selected by Governor Aycock for that purpose.

Broadnax shot and killed Sidney Blair, a man 60 years of age and wounded Miss Walker, a school teacher on the night of March 20th. This took place in the Carmel section of Rockingham county, and because of the fear of a lynching he was brought to Raleigh for safe keeping.

Broadnax was in charge of Deputy Sheriff J. C. Faucette yesterday when the afternoon train was taken for Reidsville, and it was Deputy Faucette who captured him immediately after the shooting. Broadnax appeared entirely indifferent about the matter yesterday.

Being asked if he killed Mr. Blair and shot Miss Walker he answered "Yes, I did it." "What caused you to shoot them?" was next asked him "Because Nat Fuller asked me to do it," was his answer, and that was the only reason he gave.

Deputy Faucette said that matters were quiet in Reidsville and that there was no thought of lynching there when Broadnax was brought back for trial. The speedy action of Governor Aycock in ordering a special term has had much to do with allaying any desire for an execution by Judge Lynch.

MOB CHASED NEGRO
Disorderly Whites and Blacks Fight In Bridgeville.
Bridgeville, Sept. 7.—In a riot here at midnight Saturday night, Edward Smith, white, was stabbed, and several negroes badly beaten. Smith was standing at a pump in front of the store of A. W. Culver when Joseph Andrews, a negro, slipped up behind him and stabbed him in the leg.

Andrews then ran into Culver's store. A mob quickly formed, armed with shotguns and revolvers. The men surrounded the store and wrecked the interior in an effort to capture the negro. But Andrews escaped by a rear door and, dodging a shower of bullets, escaped after being pursued a mile.

Several negroes, who went to Andrews' assistance, were beaten by the whites.

It is believed that some of the shots took effect on Andrews, as several blood spots were seen along the railroad track whence he fled.

The board of aldermen of Port Gibson has passed an order requiring every property owner on Church and College streets and some on cross streets to build a six-foot brick pavement. The work is to be done in 60 days, else the board will have it done and collect the cost as taxes are collected. The order has created the biggest stir the town has enjoyed for many years, and petitions and counter-petitions are flying thick and fast. The Reveille believes the order would be a good one were it not so radical. There are people who are absolutely unable to comply with the demand. Some of these are widows with but small income. If the board would modify the order so that it would not be so drastic, we are sure that the tirade of opposition would go up into smoke. A complete repeal of the order, however, without a substitute, would be a great mistake.

Several plans have been suggested, and we hope the aldermen can substitute one of them: First, if the order could be supplimented by a clause giving property owners the privilege of using a cheaper material than brick, but specifying that the work thus done shall be under the supervision of the marshal; Second, that a special sidewalks tax be levied and the paving be done by the town, from year to year; Third, that the town buy a quantity of brick and give any one the privilege of using them to build sidewalks.

We appreciate the board's effort to improve the town, and, while we hope that the present order will not be enforced as it stands, we do not want to see the matter entirely dropped.

The statement of the town's financial condition, which appears elsewhere, makes a much better showing than the Reveille expected. There is more money in the treasury than there has been at this time of year for many years past; and there is every indication that with judicious management, the next statement, twelve months hence, will show even a better condition.

Now that the people's minds have been set at rest along this line, let us have an answer to the questions propounded by "Citizen" in to-day's Reveille. We know that the board has no hesitancy in making these things public, and since the questions have been asked, no harm can come of answering them.

Bishop Galloway has again placed himself on record as opposing statutory prohibition, on the ground that he believes in keeping the question free from politics. The views of Judge Truly, as expressed in the jury charge, have a special significance in view of the general agitation of the race problem, and the recent troubles with the whitecappers in that section of the state. A portion of his address is as follows:

"Gentlemen—I desire to say a few plain words to you about the race question, as it is called, the labor question as it really is with us.

"I think it is time, high time, that some one in the state of Mississippi should say something on this line to the people. Some one who speaks the truth in fear of God. Someone who has nothing to lose by speaking the truth, nothing to gain by concealing it. Someone whose sincerity cannot reasonably be questioned; who can have no other motive than the bettering of the condition of his people—the advancement of the prosperity and welfare of his country.

"And, first, gentlemen, it should ever be borne in mind that the race question is rarely agitated either north or south save by some designing office seeker who hopes to achieve political success as a result. If this agitation occurs in the North, you will find, generally, if not invariably, that it is with the desire and expectation of solidifying the negro vote throughout the Northern states by appealing to and inflaming the passions of the negroes by some chimerical scheme of social equality, or by a promise of political preferment to some of their number. If in the South the desire for political aggrandisement is the same, and the agitator hopes to achieve the desired end by arousing in the white man the racial prejudice against the negro by appealing to his animosities which should, for the good of both races, be allowed to remain dormant. But whether North or South, public office is the desired goal, only different roads are chosen to arrive at the same end. It is well for us to look at this question squarely and candidly, and if we do, we are irresistably driven to the conclusion that that man, no matter what his station in life, who willfully disturbs the amicable relationship now existing between landlord and tenant, employer and employe, is an enemy to the peace of society, and as such should be rebuked by every patriotic, conservative, God-fearing man who has had the best interests of his country and his people at heart.

"Our state is prospering, our people happy and contented; fertile fields are tilled by contented farmers, tenants and laborers, and the products of their toil bring fair compensation in the marts of the world.

"I repeat, therefore, that any man who tries, in private or in public utterances, to disturb in this connection the existing order of things is a discordant element and a menace to the peace and happiness of our country.

"Do we realize or have we paused to consider that the negroes are not in our midst by their own volition or by our choice? Do we realize that neither race is responsible for the presence of the other? We must deal with the existing order of things as we found them, and both races being here, is it not true, undeniably true, that to a great extent the prosperity of one race depends upon the other.

"The negro looks to us for his rights under the law, for protection from oppression, for common justice and fair play; he asks that he be allowed to work out his racial salvation in his own way. In this state at least he has no dream of social equality; he makes no demand for the ballot. That this is true one only need refer to the incontrovertable fact

Then why this recent agitation against the negro; this outbreak of whitecapping and terrorizing? What cause, what excuse is there? It is urged that the negro is ignorant and often vicious-in his ignorance. Granted that this be true, is it not then our duty as far-sighted, patriotic citizens to relieve this condition by lessening his ignorance? Did you ever study the history of civilization and fail to be impressed by the fact that it is only after twenty centuries of Christian education that our own race has reached its present high pinnacle? Will he condemn him for his ignorance and then take away from him the only method by which his condition can be improved, his lawlessness decreased, his vice diminished, his usefulness increased? Condemn his ignorance and then decree that he shall remain in ignorance?

"It is urged that it is money wasted to educate the negro. I say to you that it is money well invested, for it pays you, the taxpayers, large dividends in decreased crime, in shorter terms of court, in a better citizenship. The harvest moon has dwindled—they have housed the corn and rye.
And now the idle reapers lounge against the bolted doors;
Without are hungry harvesters, within enchanted stores.

Lo! they had bread while they were out a-toiling in the sun;
Now they are strolling beggars, for the harvest work is done.
They are the gods of husbandry; they gather in the sheaves,

They know the noon, they know the pitiless rain before the morn;
They know the sweep of furrowed fields that darken in the gloom—
A little while their hope on earth, then evermore their tomb.

STONED HER SCHOOL.
Topeka Woman's Exciting Experience in Mississippi.
Mrs. H. I. Miller, of this city, who is principal of Lincoln school at Meridian, Miss., had an experience with a mob of "southern gentlemen," which stoned the house occupied by the teachers of the school at 2705 Eleventh street, Meridian. The occurrence took place last Thursday. Several shutters and windows in the house were smashed out.

Lincoln school is a colored school with an attendance of about 500, established under the auspices of the American Missionary association of New York. It was organized by Mrs. Miller ten years ago, and was the first school of the kind to be established in Meridian for the education of colored children.

The mob was incited by articles in the Meridian Star, a typical "niggerhating" Mississippi newspaper. The Star has been hostile to the purposes of Lincoln school ever since its establishment. The attitude of President Roosevelt on the negro question, and his open friendship for Booker Washington has caused the Star to indulge in very violent editorials and much distorted news matter. Wednesday night the Star contained a double-leaded editorial advising the people of the city to drive out the northerners who were teaching colored schools in the south. The next night the mob attacked the teachers' home. Mrs. Miller was the only teacher there, as school has not yet commenced, and none of those in charge of the school had arrived with the exception of Mrs. Miller, who went to Meridian a few weeks ago to supervise the preparation of the buildings for the year's work.

Mrs. Miller was of course greatly alarmed by the action of the mob, but did nothing except stay indoors, out of range of the missiles. When the cowardly rioters grew tired of stoning the house, they dispersed.

The following day the Star contained a flaring account of the affair, and stated that the lady principal of the school dashed out at the mob and fired several shots at the citizens who were venting their "righteous indignation."

Mrs. Miller states in a letter received by Topeka friends that she has written a letter to the mayor of Meridian, appealing to him for protection, and that she thinks the school will not be molested. There is a large school building and a chapel on the Lincoln school grounds. The teachers' home is situated some distance from the school.

Meridian, Miss., with is mob of stone-throwing citizens, seems to be very much akin to Pekin, where the boxers attacked the civilized missionaries and ministerial headquarters.

LATTER DRIVEN AWAY
NEW YORK, May 5.—Several hundred Italian strikers made a demonstration today before the diggers and shovelers employed on the Muscoot dam, at the waterworks improvements, in the borough of the Bronx, and succeeded in driving them from their work. The laborers at work on the dam for Contractor John B. McDonald had announced their satisfaction with the wages paid, and said they would not strike. But the strikers, who have harassed the McDonald contracts, especially along the subway, said they would drive the men from the trenches, and they appeared at the dam several hundred strong.

The first laborers to start to work were hooted and howled at. A few stones were thrown, and, as the number of laborers increased, a leader in the crowd of strikers shouted a phrase in Italian, and a dash was made upon the works. The laborers dropped their tools and fled. Not wishing to mix with the police, who had been called, the strikers dispersed. Police kept all strikers moving today along the route of the subway and, with the numerous officers on guard, there was a line of blue in Broadway from 42d street to 100th street. Strikers were not allowed to gather at street corners even to discuss their trouble. The strikers had 400 pickets along the line of work. A number of ironworkers employed in the subway were forced to quit work today by a lack of material and the men to fetch it.

In the Greenpoint section of Brooklyn the police had a lively encounter with a gang of about twenty Italian strikers who yesterday quit work on an excavation. The strikers attacked the new men today and the police charged the assailants, using their clubs freely. The police of this district were also called upon to protect men who took the places of striking teamsters.

Upward of 500 hands employed at the Planet carpet mills, Brooklyn, went on strike today for shorter hours.

At Mt. Vernon today between 300 and 400 Italian laborers who have been on strike since last week marched to where sixty negroes were at work and persuaded them to quit and join the strikers. The strikers then marched around the city and succeeded in getting practically all laborers to quit until they came to where an Italian contractor is building a sewer. The contractor sent for the police, who are now guarding the men at work.

Strike at Philadelphia Spreads.

PHILADELPHIA, Pa., May 5.—The Brotherhood of Carpenters, whose members have been on strike since May 1, for an eight-hour working day and in increase in wages amounting to 50 cents a day, although not affiliated with the council of allied building trades, has united with that body to oppose the Master Builders' Exchange. This action, it is said, is taken with a view to preventing a lockout by the master builders, and resulted from the announcement last night by officials of the Master Plasterers' Association that efforts would be made to fill with non-union men the places of the 200 plasterers' laborers who struck yesterday. The plasterers' laborers are affiliated with the council. The coalition will result in the refusal of the carpenters to return to work, even though their demands are granted, if non-union men are employed by the contracting plasterers or employers in other building trades whose men may strike during the present crisis.

The brotherhood, therefore, in the present dispute is pledged to the sympathetic support of the council, whose affiliated unions insist on the sympathetic strike clause being inserted in all wage scale agreements with employers.

Strike Situation at Omaha.

OMAHA, Neb., May 5.—The strike of the teamsters and restaurant men is beginning to be felt keenly by business interests. Not a ton of coal is being delivered, and the wholesale houses are unable to handle their wares to and from freight depots. A number of large buildings have been compelled to shut down elevator service, several factories are contemplating closing down for want of fuel and at the hotels the same difficulty is being experienced.

To add to the seriousness of the situation, the teamsters have added 100 more men to their ranks and the Horseshoers' Union has voted not to shoe horses driven by non-union men.

POLICE UNABLE TO COPE WITH FURIOUS STRIKERS.
Compel Negroes Who Took Their Places to Join Union in Terror of Death—Drive Others From Work—Are Camping in Woods—More Trouble Feared To-day.

MOUNT VERNON, N. Y., May 5.—A mob of 250 striking Italians who were employed by the T. E. Crimmins, the New York contractor, in relaying the tracks of the Union trolley road, marched through the streets of Mount Vernon and Pelham to-day, armed with clubs and pickaxes, and compelled nearly all of the other Italians employed in those places to quit work.

The strikers completely outnumbered the local police and this afternoon Chief Foley had to call out the reserves. They were sent to the home of William Archer, the New York contractor, who owns a mansion at Corcoran Manor in one of the finest sections of Mount Vernon, to protect a gang of men who were grading his grounds.

Murder at Piedmont.
On Tuesday night, June 30th, an old negro man named Reuben Elrod, was shot to death at his home in Anderson County, about one mile from Piedmont. Old Uncle Reube was born and reared in this settlement, and has been a familiar personage about Piedmont ever since the place was founded. He was always ready to do odd jobs of every kind, and was considered a kind of inoffensive man. The one bad feature about him was that he had the reputation of keeping a lot of loose negro women about his place, and this, it seems, led to his undoing as near as we can gather from the evidence given at the coroner's inquest.

It seems that sometime on Tuesday night a company of men came to old Reuben's cabin and demanded the women who were in the house. In the wrangle that ensued a shot was fired through the weatherboarding of the house at random, but the ball struck old Reuben in the throat, cut his jugular vein and caused his death. His body fell on a lighted lamp he held in his hand, and he was burned somewhat about the neck and shoulders. The two negro women who were in the house claim that they were badly beaten with sticks and ordered to leave the country. The women were evidently cowed, and could not o. would not swear to the identity of any of the assailants. Macon, Ga., Aug. 7.—After being lynched by a mob and left for dead, "Sam" Johnson, the negro accused of assaulting a white woman near Helena, Ga., lives to tell the story. Johnson was hanged to a tree by a mob on Tuesday night. Soon after the mob departed, some negroes came along and cut down the swinging body. Life appeared to be extinct, but after the rope was removed from the man's neck he showed signs of life and soon revived.

Johnson was brought to the outskirts of Macon and secreted in a hut, where he was found to-day by health officers, who had been told that a negro there was suffering from a contagious disease. Taken from the Officers by Angry Farmers, Hanged to a Tree and His Body Riddled.
GENERAL ATTACK ON NEGROES
CONSTRUCTION GANG ROUTED AND MANY OF THE MEN WOUNDED.
Their Camp Burned by the Mob—Texas Negro Lynched for an Assault on a Mere Baby.
THEBES, Ill., April 26.—An unknown negro, aged about seventeen years, was lynched by a mob of angry farmers near the village of Santa Fe, this afternoon, for trying to assault the ten-year-old daughter of farmer Branson Davis, and this was followed by a general onslaught upon a colony of negroes living in tents who were engaged in bridge construction work. The tents were burned and many negroes were shot, but so far as known, none was killed. Hundreds of shots were exchanged, but no whites were hurt.

Branson Davis lives one-half mile east of Santa Fe, a small village near here. While his ten-year-old daughter was in the barnyard, to-day, the negro accosted her. She ran but he seized her and her screams brought her mother to her rescue. The negro fled. Officers were notified and were soon in pursuit. News of the assault speedily spread among the neighboring farmers, and an angry mob started in search of the assailant.

The negro was captured by officers and was being brought to Santa Fe when the mob of farmers was met. A scrimmage resulted, during which the farmers secured the negro. He confessed the crime but begged for mercy. Without a word the mob started with the prisoner toward the new bridge being constructed across the Mississippi, where he was hanged to an oak tree without ceremony or delay. After the body dangled in the air a few minutes it was riddled with bullets.

The officers endeavored to disperse the mob, but their efforts were unavailing.

A rush was made for a colony of several hundred negroes employed on bridge construction work and living in tents near the bridge. The negroes saw the mob coming and opened fire. A fusillade followed and the whites fired with effect, as many of the negroes were shot down. None of the mob was injured and it is not known how seriously the negroes were wounded. The mob pressed forward, notwithstanding the steady fire until the negroes turned and fled toward a near-by wood, taking their wounded with them. The mob then fell on the tents and burned them. After accomplishing a general work of destruction, the mob dispersed. Extra police were sworn in and to-night the village is under heavy guard. Excitement is intense.

Santa Fe is a village in the extreme southwestern portion of Illinois, near the Chicago & Eastern Illinois Railroad.

Negro Pastor Thomas Informed Colonel Oglesby Two Days Before Wyatt Was Hanged.
REPUBLIC SPECIAL.
Springfield, Ill., June 25.—Colonel John D. Oglesby, private secretary to the Governor, was in error when he rebuked the Reverend C. H. Thomas, pastor of the African Methodist Episcopal Church at Belleville. In a speech in Chicago Mr. Thomas said he wrote to Governor Yates preceding the Belleville lynching, warning the executive of the condition of affairs existing there.

Colonel Oglesby in his communication denied that a letter had been received at the executive office from Thomas, and demanded a retraction of the statements made concerning Governor Yates.

But Thomas's letter, written June 2 last, has turned up in the Attorney General's office, and bears the file mark of the executive office, together with the date of its arrival, June 3. The letter was found upon a desk in the Attorney General's office, but there was no other communication with it. The original, bearing the executive file mark, has been preserved.

Thomas's letter, written on June 2, preceded the lynching of Wyatt, which did not occur until the night of June 6, by four days. Thomas had received an anonymous communication warning him to leave Belleville, and this, together with the other warnings, induced his communication of warning to Governor Yates. The warning to Thomas to leave Belleville, a copy of which is contained in his letter to Yates, is as follows:

WARNING TO THOMAS.

"St. Louis, Mo.: Charles Thomas, Colored—You have now drawn the color line and are trying to force the niggers on the white race. You are well aware that a nigger was not born to equal the whites. So, being you want to force matters, I will tell you plain, and you may take gospel heed that if you do not leave Belleville in two weeks you will, with your bravados, meet your place in line with other good niggers. So you may take this timely warning and go where the niggers have more rights than Belleville.

"This is no joke, but a plain warning, so if you fail to go then take the result.

"A CITIZEN."

The original of this copy was mailed to me the twenty-second day of May, and the time for the trouble to begin is June 5.

REVEREND C. H. THOMAS.

PAID WITH HIS LIFE
MOB WREAKED ITS FURY UPON A NEGRO.
AFTER COURT HAD FINED HIM
WHITE MEN DECIDED TO VISIT EXTREME PENALTY.
Fambro Was Shot and Killed in His Home Near Griffin—About Fifteen White Men Did the Work. Efforts Will be Made to Bring Them to Justice—Fambro's Offense Had Been an Indecent Exposure. Was Fined $40—Was Working Out Fine for Man Who Paid It.

Griffin, Ga., Feb. 24.—Will Fambro, a negro, was shot to death this morning by a party of unknown white men at this home half a mile beyond Spalding Mills.

The crime was one of the most unwarranted in the annals of Spalding county. About 2 o'clock this morning a party of about 15 men emerged from the woods near the negro's home and opened fire with shotguns and Winchester, shooting hundreds of holes in the building.

They then advanced to the front door and demanded admittance, which was refused by the negro's wife. A panel was broken out of the door, and through this opening several guns were thrust and fired into the room. Evidently one of the first shots fired struck Fambro in the right breast, and he staggered across the room and fell dead in the kitchen adjoining.

The men were unaware of the fact that they had killed their victim, and again demanded of his wife that she get him out of the house, threatening to set fire to the building in case she refused to do so.

Tried to Save Him.

H. F. Thurman, on whose place the tragedy occurred, hurried out near the scene, but being unarmed, he was unable to prevent the killing. He called to the crowd, but they paid no attention to him until the woman was told that help would soon reach her. This frightened the mob, and it withdrew to the woods, keeping up a continual fire until lost to view.

It was not until daylight that the full extent of the damage done by the mob was discovered, as the negro's family ran to another house for safety as soon as the party dispersed, leaving the dead man in the house.

The crime for which the negro paid such severe penalty was committed early in January. He was at that time driving a dray for the Spalding Mills, and while drunk made an indecent exposure.

Fined, but This Not Enough.

He was arrested and at the January term of the Superior Court pleaded guilty, and was sentenced to pay a fine of $40. Mr. Thurman paid the fine, and Fambro was working it out.

There had been threats made against the negro, but it was not thought these would be carried out, as he had evidently been sufficiently punished for his crime.

Last night's violence is greatly regretted, and it is said that a determined effort will be made to apprehend the guilty parties.
william-fambro-griffin-1903-02-23.A11:
TIME TO CALL A HALT.
The people of the entire state are profoundly interested in having the members of the mob that murdered the negro at Griffin at an early hour on Tuesday morning sought out and brought to justice. As reported in our dispatches the crime was a cruel and cold-blooded one. The negro had been arrested for an offense committed while drunk—an offense for which he was, as was right, promptly punished, notwithstanding the fact that he was drunk when he committed it. He was heavily fined and discharged, his employer having paid his fine.

The offense was committed more than a month ago and the negro had no reason to suspect that he was in danger from mob violence. He had been tried and was paying the penalty that had been passed upon him. He was working out his fine. What excuse, therefore, was there for the mob that went to his house and deliberately shot him to death?

Public sentiment seems to justify lynch law when the victim of it is guilty of assaulting a woman, especially when the lynching follows quickly the commission of the crime, but there is no public sentiment that upholds such a lynching as that of Griffin.

What is the grand jury of Spalding county going to do about it? That is a question that, no doubt, is being generally asked. We feel safe in saying that if every man concerned in the killing of that negro were arrested and punished to the fullest extent of the law there would be rejoicing throughout the state. The county authorities ought to make every effort to discover the guilty parties, and the Governor ought to assist them by offering a reward for the apprehension of each and every one of them. The county and the state ought to be made too hot for them to remain within the limits of either with anything approaching comfort, even if it be found impossible to get sufficient evidence against them to convict them of the crime of which they are guilty.

If mob violence in cases like this is permitted to pass unpunished and unnoticed it will not be long before it will become common in the most ordinary offenses, and the victims of it will not be confined to negroes. Besides, the people of Georgia cannot regard with indifference such glaring injustice. It is their intention that the negroes shall have all the protection that the law gives them, and it is their duty to see to it that the justice dealt out to them is as even-handed as that dealt out to the white people. If irresponsible white men take the law into their own hands with entire impunity we shall soon have a sad condition of affairs in this state.

The Griffin tragedy should not be permitted to drop out of sight. The county authorities and the Governor should not be satisfied until all means for bringing the criminals to justice are exhausted. We have courts and all the machinery for the protection of life and property. Let us see to it that the law is respected.

REWARD OFFERED FOR THE MURDERERS.
Governor Wants Men Who Killed Negroes Apprehended.
Atlanta, Feb. 26.—Two cases, in which negroes were shot down without apparent cause, by unknown lawless white persons, were brought to the attention of Governor Terrell today, and the Governor offered a reward of $250 in each case, for the arrest with proof to convict, of the parties responsible for the murders.

One of the most outrageous cases is told of in the affidavit of Solicitor General John Bennett of the Brunswick Circuit. On the night of Feb. 7, a party of negroes were having a dance about two miles from McDonald's mill in Coffee county, when unknown white persons appeared at the two doors of the building and fired a fusilade upon the dancers, killing Alex Mervin and Sambo Bell, and wounding nine others, some seriously and some slightly.

After the rest of the negroes had fled in fear, the murderers entered the building, tied the bodies of the wounded to those of the dead and then robbed the dead and living of all the money they could find on their persons.

The usual reward for a person charged with murder is $150, but in this case the Governor made it $250 for each.

The other case in which similar rewards were offered was that of the murder of Will Fambro in Spalding county on the night of Feb. 23, last Monday. Fambro insulted a lady and child while intoxicated. He was arrested, pleaded guilty and was fined $40, which was paid. On Monday night, an angry mob of white men went to his home and fired a fusilade into the dwelling, killing Fambro and terrifying his wife and children.

The Governor has offered a reward of $250 for the arrest of each of the murderers.
