DEATH FROM A MOB
NARROWLY ESCAPED BY WILLIAM HARDY, A NEGRO,
WHO SHOT RAYMOND MULLINS
MITCHELL COUNTY WAS STIRRED UP OVER THE SHOOTING.
Mullins Was a Member of a Posse That Went to Hardy's House to Arrest Him—As Mullins Entered Hardy Fired—Only by Taking the Negro to Albany Was It Thought That His Safety Could Be Assured. Negro Was Wounded.

Albany, Ga., Nov. 22.—Raymond Mullins, a prominent young man of Baconton, Mitchell county, was shot and mortally wounded about 10 o'clock this morning by William Hardy, a negro.

Hardy narrowly escaped lynching, the tragedy causing great excitement throughout the upper portion of Mitchell county. Hardy was hurried away from Baconton early this afternoon and is now in jail here.

When shot, young Mullins was a member of a small posse which had been hurriedly organized for the purpose of arresting Hardy. The latter had been beating his wife earlier in the morning, and she appealed to the officers for protection. The marshal went to the house occupied by Hardy and undertook to arrest him, but was informed by the negro that he would not be taken unless killed. The officer was unarmed, and hurried away and called several persons to his assistance, at the same time procuring a Winchester rifle.

Returning to Hardy's house, the party forced open the front door and entered. The negro was evidently expecting an attack, for he fired on the first man to enter, which happened to be Mullins. The young man was shot through the abdomen, and at last report was dying.

Hardy made a dash from the house and several shots were fired after him. One struck him in the leg, and a bullet from the marshal's rifle passed through his shoulder. He ran a few steps further, but was easily captured. In a short time it was evident that a mob was in process of organizing, and that the negro would be lynched unless the authorities took steps to remove him. A telephone message was sent to Albany for Sheriff Edward, who started for Baconton in a buggy. Four miles from this place he met a party having Hardy in charge.

The negro was placed in the sheriff's buggy and brought on to the city, where he was lodged in jail. He declares that he was drunk when he did the shooting, and remembers nothing of it.

Young Mullins was one of the most prominent young men in Mitchell county, a son of Mayor Mullins of Baconton. He went to help arrest Hardy against his father's expressed wishes.

MURDERED IN COURT
NEW YORK NEGRO KILLS AN ANTI-POLICY AGENT.
Threatened With Lynching, the Murderer Was Hurried Away and Immediately Indicted.
A dispatch from New York announces the murder there yesterday of Charles F. McFarlane of the Anti-Policy Society, who was shot and killed on the general sessions floor of the Criminal Courts building by William Spencer, a negro who was to have been placed on trial on the charge of violating the anti-policy law. A detective who witnessed the shooting knocked the revolver from Spencer's hand and placed him under arrest.

Four shots were fired by Spencer, three of which took effect in McFarlane's body, and the fourth hit Philip E. Bray, also a member of the Anti-Policy Society, in the arm, inflicting a slight wound. Mr. McFarlane was superintendent of the Anti-Policy Society.

The case was almost immediately taken before the grand jury, and less than two hours after the death of McFarlane Spencer had been indicted for murder in the first degree and sent to the Toombs.

After the shooting the crowds in the courtrooms flocked into the corridors and the greatest excitement prevailed. A crowd of men uttering cries of "Lynch him!" and "Throw him over the balcony!" attempted to take the prisoner from the detective. It required a strong force of police to save the negro from the fury of the men and disperse the crowd.

Bray was taken downstairs to the police station, where Spencer had been held. The prisoner looked at him as he was taken behind the sergeant's desk and gently placed in a chair.

"Is that the man who shot you and shot McFarlane?" asked the sergeant.

Bray's face twitched with pain. It was fully a minute before he spoke. He just glanced up at the negro, who stood looking at him stoically, and then he said:

"Yes, that's the man; take him away."

"What have you to say—why did you shoot him?" asked County Detective McClellan.

"They testified against me," he muttered. One of the detectives said, loud enough for him to hear:

"Take the — up to headquarters quick."

The negro turned and gave the man a look in which there was unmistakable rage and hatred. Spencer, as he stood confronting Bray, looked just like the typical Tenderloin negro. He was perhaps better dressed than the average of his class.

While Spencer was being arraigned there was a great crowd around the building. Fresh cries of "Lynch the nigger! Lynch him!" were heard on all sides. The crowd had by this time become so great that the Center street cars were blocked for a time.

The prisoners in the new Toombs had a full view of the mob. They also yelled and shouted and made a general uproar. Warden Van de Carr had to send an additional number of keepers to quiet them.

Spencer was taken to police headquarters by Detective Sergeants McNaught, Daly and Brown. At first he refused to talk, but after a while he said:

"This man has been hounding me on the street. He has called me a black — and has threatened to lick me. I told him he might lick a white man, but he couldn't lick me. He has told lies in lots of cases. I might just as well go for something as for nothing. I'm no chicken-hearted nigger. I don't care if I go to the chair tomorrow."
william-spencer-new-york-1903-06-15.A3:
TRIED TO LYNCH THE MURDERER Prompt Action on Part of Police Alone Saved Negro, Who Shot and Killed White Man, From Immediate Death SHOOTING OCCURRED IN CROWDED COURT ROOM Victim Was Charles F. McFarlane, Superintendent of the Anti-Policy Society—The Negro Promptly Indicted for Murder
New York, June 15.—Charles F. McFarlane, of the Anti-Policy Society, was shot and killed today, on the general sessions floor of the criminal court building, by William Spencer, a negro, who was to have been placed on trial today on the charge of violating the anti-policy law. A detective witnessed the shooting, and, knocking the revolver from Spencer's hand, placed him under arrest.

Four shots in all were fired, two of which struck McFarlane in the head. The third penetrated his heart and the fourth hit Philip E. Bray, also a member of the Anti-Policy Society, in the arm, inflicting a slight wound. McFarlane was superintendent of the Anti-Policy Society.

The negro told the police that McFarlane has been following him and telling lies about him. Spencer said that he had met McFarlane in the elevator on the way to the general sessions floor and had asked him to stop talking about him. McFarlane, the negro said, swore at him. As soon as he stepped out of the elevator Spencer shot McFarlane from behind. To Inspector McCluskey he said: "I am no chicken-hearted nigger. I thought I might as well go for something as nothing. I don't care if I go to the electric chair tomorrow.

At least 20 persons witnessed the shooting. The case was almost immediately taken before the grand jury and less than two hours after the death of McFarlane, Spencer had been indicted for murder in the first degree.

After the shooting the crowds in the courtroom flocked into the corridors and the greatest excitement prevailed. A crowd of men attempted to take the prisoner from the detective, fighting fiercely to reach him. A dozen policemen who were in the building surrounded Spencer and saved him from the fury of the men. Not until an additional squad arrived could the crowd be dispersed.

Spencer was arraigned before Recorder Goff and was given until tomorrow to plead. District Attorney Jerome said he would move for trial a week from today.
william-spencer-new-york-1903-06-15.A4:
POLICY PLAYER KILLS.
INDICTED HOUR LATER.
Negro Shoots Macfarlane in Criminal Courts Building.
Fulfilling the threat he made last Friday, "You'll never go on the stand to testify against me," William Spencer, a negro ex-convict, yesterday, a few moments before the time set for his trial for having policy slips, shot and instantly killed Superintendent Charles F. Macfarlane, of Captain F. Norton Goddard's Anti-Policy Society, in the corridor of the second floor of the Criminal Courts Building.

An hour afterward he was indicted for murder in the first degree by the grand jury and arraigned before Recorder Goff, and District Attorney Jerome gave notice that he would move for trial in a week.

Macfarlane in telling a friend of the threat had said:

"I don't like the way that coon spoke. I think he may try to shoot me."

One bullet pierced his brain and issued from his head. Another lodged in the brain and a third in his heart. A fourth bullet struck Philip E. Bray, of No. 369 West Forty-eighth-st., also an Anti-Policy Society agent, in the left arm.

The corridor was crowded at the time, and in a few minutes the building was in an uproar. The noise of the firing was heard plainly in all parts of the building, and in many cases proceedings in the courtrooms were stopped temporarily, nearly every one rushing into the corridors to find out what had happened.

TOOK DELIBERATE AIM.

Spencer has been arrested several times for playing policy or having slips. Macfarlane had testified against the man several times, and Spencer had a grudge against him. Macfarlane and Bray entered the building by the Centre-st. entrance just before 11 a. m. They took an elevator to the second floor. Spencer was waiting in the corridor. As soon as he saw Macfarlane he walked over to him and began talking. Bray walked a few steps ahead and began to talk with George Simpson, of the law firm of Levy & Unger. They heard Macfarlane utter an exclamation, and then they saw him walking away from the negro.

When Macfarlane reached them, he and Bray began walking toward the Part III, General Sessions, courtroom. Simpson turned to walk the other way and he saw Spencer pointing a revolver at Macfarlane. The lawyer uttered a cry and Macfarlane turned his head slightly to the left. Just as he did so two shots rang out and two bullets struck Macfarlane on the left side of the head. He spun around until he faced the negro for about a second. Spencer fired a third and a fourth shot. The third shot went to Macfarlane's heart, and as he fell the fourth shot went over him and into Bray's arm.

Simpson said afterward:

"The negro was as cool as a cucumber. He had one eye shut and was taking aim when I saw him first, and then I dropped on the floor, as I did not want to run the risk of having any of the shots hit me."

Spencer still had his hand raised as if to fire after the fourth shot, but he was seized simultaneously by Detective Tunney, of the Oak-st. station, and Roundsman Kelleher, of the Richards-st. station, Brooklyn. County Detective Reardon knocked the pistol out of his hand and took him by the throat.

A hurry call for an ambulance was sent to the Hudson Street Hospital. Dr. Marshall, after examining Macfarlane's body, said he had died at once. Bray had fainted and fallen on the floor beside the body. Dr. Marshall revived him and then Spencer was taken before him.

"Is this the man who shot you?" asked Detective Sergeant McNaught, who was holding the negro.

"Yes, that's him," said Bray, weakly, "Take him away and kill him."

By this time about five hundred persons had packed the corridor and the policemen had a hard time making them move along. There were about twenty-five negroes in the crowd.

Assistant District Attorney Rand appeared on the scene and at once took charge of the case. He got all the witnesses that were necessary and then sent word to the Coroner's office on the ground floor to have a coroner view the body and give a permit for its removal. A coroner did not appear until over a half an hour later. In that time about a thousand persons gazed at the body lying in a big pool of blood.

WILLING TO GO TO ELECTRIC CHAIR.

Spencer, at Police Headquarters, said he was thirty-five years old, and lived at No. 224 West Twenty-ninth-st. He admitted the shooting and in a cold, matter of fact way said to Inspector McClusky:

"I'm no chicken hearted nigger. I thought I might as well go for something as nothing. I don't care if I go to the electric chair to-morrow."

A messenger was sent to find Captain Goddard, but it was learred he was out of town. District Attorney Jerome arrived at his office a few minutes after the shooting, and was told of what had happened.

Spencer has served two years and a half in Sing Sing for burglary and attempted assault and twice for policy playing.

In one of the back pockets of Macfarlane's trousers was a pearl handled revolver, fully loaded.

Macfarlane lived at No. 136 Edgecombe-ave. with his wife and his two-year-old daughter. He was thirty-eight years old. He was once a deputy under ex-Elections Superintendent John McCullagh. Before that he had held a position with the Metropolitan Street Railway Company. Macfarlane had been three years with the society and had taken the place of Edward Reardon, who resigned as superintendent to enter the District Attorney's office. Reardon was one of those who helped carry Macfarlane's body to the coroners' office.

The negro also wounded Philip E. Bray, a detective of the society, who was with Macfarlane.

Spencer served more than two years in jail, eighteen years ago for burglary. He has been arrested repeatedly for operating the policy game. It was in a place managed by Spencer that a shot was fired, presumably at Frank Moss, counsel for the society, during a raid on June 8, last. Spencer has always had the reputation of being quiet and self-controlled, although sullen. He was arrested by Supt. Macfarlane on May 11, this year, charged with running an independent policy game among the negro tenements on the West Side.

When Al Adams went to State prison, the big game which had been under his management broke into small independent enterprises, conducted by his former employees on their own responsibility. None of these men made as much money as they used to be paid under the Adams system, and they have done some ugly talking about what they would do to the officers and men of the anti-policy society if they ever had the chance. Spencer did rather more than his share of this threatening. His trial was set for yesterday morning.

Supt. Macfarlane, with Detective Bray, stepped out of one of the elevators on the east side of the building and there met George Simpson, a lawyer. The three walked toward Part IV. of the Court of General Sessions, where Spencer's case was to be tried. Spencer stepped out of a group of four negroes who were lounging against the rail of the gallery opposite the elevator and approached Macfarlane.

"I see you are here, Spencer," said Macfarlane, smiling. Spencer had been out on bail.

"Yes," growled Spencer, "and I see you are here."
He swung on his heel and walked three or four paces ahead of Macfarlane, Bray and Simpson. He is a big fellow, with a round, chocolate-brown face and rather clean-cut features. Before he had passed the top of the stairway, which adjoins the elevator shaft, he swung around, slipped a revolver from his pocket, pointed it at Macfarlane's head and fired. The muzzle of the revolver was within two feet of Macfarlane.

Macfarlane and Simpson swayed and fell to the floor together. As they were falling, the negro fired two more shots. The lawyer, as soon as he struck the floor, scrambled to his feet and ran into the crowd of people who were scuttling for their lives all over the corridor. The halls of the building are always full on Monday mornings. Bray stumbled backward against a post.

The negro walked up to Macfarlane, who lay on his back, took deliberate aim and fired again, the shot entering Macfarlane's breast and presumably piercing his heart.

By this time all the second floor of the building was in a riot. Men and women were running without any definite idea of where they were going. Folks came boiling out of the court rooms and came into violent collision with others who were trying to get in.

Spencer made a bolt for the stairs, still gripping the revolver. A court officer made a grab at him and caught him by the arm. The negro wrenched his arm away, tearing nearly all the finger nails from the officer's hand in the effort. Roundsman Kelleher, who came bounding up stairs at the sound of the first shot, made a dive at Spencer and grabbed him about the body, pinioning his arms to his side. While the negro was struggling to get loose, dropping his revolver in the scrimmage, Detective Robert McNaught came up and helped Kelleher hustle his prisoner up against the wall.

The followed a wild struggle by every uniformed and ununiformed policeman and detective in the building to get his hands on the murderer. At least fifteen announced afterward that "they" had captured the murderer.

The whole lot of them took the negro down to the prison cells in the basement of the building, followed by a curious and shoving, loud-talking crowd.

It was found that Bray had been shot through the arm. Macfarlane was dead. The wound in his head was enough to have killed him without the other. It had torn off nearly half of the upper part of his skull. The body lay in a pool of blood on the floor for thirty-five minutes until a Coroner could be found to survey it. The Coroner's office is on the ground floor of the building.

Detective Bray was taken down to the cells to identify Spencer and was then sent to the Hudson street hospital. When Spencer saw Bray, he said:

"Did I shoot that man? I didn't go to shoot him. I didn't know I had hit him. It was the other one I was after."

Asked why he shot Macfarlane, he said:

"He's been hounding me for seven weeks and he didn't have me right and I'd as soon go to the electric chair for doing a thing 'right' as to go to prison for something I didn't do."

The murderer was taken to Police Headquarters and then brought back to the Criminal Courts Building, where he was called upon to plead to an indictment found by the Grand Jury within one hour and thirteen minutes from the time of the murder. Recorder Goff assigned ex-Judge Wauhope Lynn as his counsel, and put the case over until to-day. The District Attorney to-day announced that he would move that the trial be set for next Monday. Deputy Assistant District Attorney Frank A. Lord will have charge of the case.

Policeman McIvor, who was also to be a witness against Spencer in the policy case, spoke to Spencer just before the shooting. Spencer said to him, sneeringly:

"They ain't again' to send me away to-day. You mark me."

Spencer made a statement at Headquarters that Macfarlane made a motion as though to shoot him and that he had acted in self-defence. When Macfarlane's body was picked up there was an umbrella tightly clutched in the right hand.

William Spencer, the negro who shot and killed Supt. Macfarlane of the Anti-Policy League in the Criminal Courts Building on June 15, was convicted last night of murder in the first degree and was sentenced by Recorder Goff to be put to death in the week beginning Aug. 17.

Although Spencer was quiet enough in court, he was violent in the prison pen downstairs between the time the jury went out and the time it reported. It was thought that some one might have slipped a knife to him, and he was searched. He resisted and broke into a violent tirade, in the course of which he threatened to kill the Recorder.

After he was subdued it was decided to handcuff him before taking him into court, but he promised to remain quiet, and the deputy sheriffs changed their mind. Half a dozen of them surrounded him, however, when he went into court to hear the verdict of the jury at 6:35. He was stolid enough when his guilt was announced.

The Recorder asked him if he had anything to say why sentence should not be pronounced at once, and he began to talk, but was cut short by his lawyer.

Spencer's counsel will probably try to get a commission appointed to inquire into his sanity. They tried on the trial to convince the jury that Spencer was insane when he shot Macfarlane and they had Drs. Prout, Ira Van Gieson, L. B. Clarke and Hyman Goodhart to swear to it. Drs. Carlos F. Yesterday morning, while on her way to Martin's Ferry, a popular and well known young lady was assaulted by a negro ruffian. The young lady is a stenographer in this city, and she will never forget yesterday morning's experience. Her home is west of Martin's Ferry, and in good weather she walks to the over-the-river city and takes a car for Wheeling. When at Locust Grove, in sight of Martin's Ferry, she met two burly negroes. One stepped in front of her and struck her a blow in the face, falling her to the ground. Fortunately she was not knocked unconscious. The brute bent over her, and his intention was criminal assault. The young lady screamed loudly several times, which frightened the two curs away. The young lady then immediately came to Martin's Ferry, running almost all the way. She informed her friends and the authorities were notified. The young lady had her glasses broken and her face slightly cut.

Chief of Police Terrill, Officer Moore, Chief of Fire Department H. Long and F. R. Sedgwick immediately drove to the scene, and Officer Moore took a cross-way so as to capture the man if he returned to town. When near the scene a negro was found asleep at the side of a fence. Chief Terrill leaped from the rig and covered the man with a revolver and made him hold up his hands until searched. He had a razor and several trinkets. He is the partner of the man who made the dastardly assault, and is in jail. The other man could not be found.

Suspect Caught.

About 8 o'clock last night, Wheeling officers arrested a suspect. Officer Norton cers arrested a suspect. Officer Norton found a negro trying doors of residences. Officer Norton started to arrest him, and he fled, with a revolver in his hand. Norton followed and ran the man to the back river. The negro ran into the river until the water almost reached his chin and then stopped. Norton leverel his gun at the man and he came to shore, dropping the revolver in the water.
